_about: The eval set. Ten vague, real-world phrasings, each in English and Mandarin,
each with the page a correct retrieval should surface.
Read by scripts/eval_queries.py, which scores hit@3 per language and prints
the table. Stage 05's DONE criterion depends on this file:
stage 05 (retrieval): hit@3 over the eval set, in Mandarin as well as English,
measured before and after the reranker.
THIS FILE IS NOT FINISHED, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.
Only 4 of the 10 queries have expect_url_contains filled in - the 4 whose target
page is confirmed present in f01_pages.json. The other 6 are null.
They are null rather than guessed because a wrong guess is worse than a blank:
an expectation naming a page that isn't in the index scores as a miss and makes
retrieval look broken when it isn't. A bare hostname ('scamwatch.gov.au') is worse
still - it scores ANY page on that domain as a hit, so the number looks great and
measures nothing.
The harness handles null: it prints those rows as UNSET with their top 3 result
URLs and leaves them out of the hit@3 denominator. Run it once, read the URLs,
paste the right slug in, re-run. The first run is what completes this file.
expect_url_contains is a SUBSTRING, not a full URL: it survives a trailing slash,
an http/https difference and a query string, and several Scamwatch pages exist
under both schemes (see stage 02's deduplication note). Use a distinctive path
segment, never a bare hostname.
The phrasings are deliberately how a senior would actually ask - vague, using the
wrong word, describing a symptom rather than naming the thing. A query set written
in the corpus's own vocabulary measures nothing: it would pass without query understanding
existing at all.
The Mandarin is the same question, not a translation of the English rewrite -
translating the ANSWER into the query is how a cross-language eval accidentally
proves nothing.
